description:
UKIVERSE is a small, passionate team from Uki tackling the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge.  

Aims to transform complex lunar and Martian mission decisions into a simple, engaging, and educational interactive experience.
summary: ASTRO: Mission Moon is a colorful browser game for children ages 7–12 that teaches space science through short, playful rescue missions. Astro, an expressive spacesuit mascot, guides children through five game types: drag and drop rescues, a supply logic grid, rover navigation, and a match three power challenge. Each level introduces a science fact, explains the results of the child’s choices, and ends with a scenario question and a clear takeaway. The lessons draw on linked NASA and Canadian Space Agency resources about life support, water recovery, power, crops, spacesuits, and radiation safety. XP, stars, badges, animations, sound effects, and an Ask Astro chat guide make learning rewarding. The current version is an MVP: all five arcade levels are open, and refreshing starts a new game.
details:
What does ASTRO do, and how does it work?
ASTRO: Mission Moon is a browser game for children ages 7–12. Children travel across a lunar mission map, predict what might happen, make choices to solve problems, see how the Moon base responds, and use what they learned when the situation changes. Astro, an expressive spacesuit mascot, guides them through seven science missions and a final challenge. An optional rescue arcade offers drag and drop, logic, rover, and match games.

What are its benefits and intended impact?
The goal is to help children understand why space systems matter, not just remember their names. Missions cover spacesuits, clean air, water recovery, power, crops, and crew safety. Feedback explains the cause of a result, while hints and retries let children learn from mistakes. The intended impact is greater curiosity about space science and more confidence in solving problems with evidence.

What did you use to build it?
ASTRO was developed as a web app using React, TypeScript, HTML, CSS, SVG, and Vite. It uses original character and map artwork, locally generated sound effects through Web Audio, and Playwright and Vitest for browser and code testing. The science explanations link to NASA and Canadian Space Agency resources. Children can play on a desktop, tablet, or phone; no special hardware or account is required.

How is it creative?
The science becomes part of a Moon rescue story. Choices affect visible system gauges, Astro reacts to what happens, and each mission asks children to apply an idea to a new situation. The illustrated route, varied game activities, sounds, XP, and badges make progress feel like an adventure.

What factors did the team consider?
The design considers scientific accuracy, age appropriate reading, clear feedback, accessibility, keyboard and touch use, reduced motion, performance on ordinary devices, and children’s privacy. Progress is saved on the device so a child can return without creating an account.
